Fitting a distributional model

Source: vignettes/fitting-a-distributional-model.Rmd
fitting-a-distributional-model.Rmd

An ordinary regression models the mean and treats everything else about the distribution as a nuisance held constant. A distributional model gives every parameter its own equation, so the scale, the shape and a zero-inflation probability may each depend on covariates, and each may be a smooth, a random effect or a penalized block.

statmod() reads one formula that carries all of them, in which a bar separates the equations, and fits it. This vignette walks through a fit and then through the functions that read it.

n <- 300
da <- data.frame(x = sort(runif(n, min = -3, max = 3)))
da$y <- rnorm(n, mean = 1 + 0.8 * da$x, sd = exp(-0.6 + 0.35 * da$x))

The scale of these data grows with x, from about 0.190.19 at x=−3x = -3 to about 1.571.57 at x=3x = 3.

A first fit

The first equation belongs to the first parameter of the distribution, so a formula with no bar models the mean and leaves the other parameters as intercepts:

f1 <- statmod(y ~ x, distrib = gaussian1_distrib(), data = da)
coef(f1)
#> $mu
#> (Intercept)           x 
#>   0.9823413   0.7605631 
#> 
#> $sigma
#> (Intercept) 
#>  -0.2493397

coef() returns one compartment per parameter, because the coefficients of the mean and of the scale are different quantities on different scales, and a single flat vector would run them together. For this model the compartment of the mean holds the coefficients of an ordinary regression, which the following check confirms:

all.equal(unname(coef(f1)$mu), unname(coef(lm(y ~ x, data = da))),
          tolerance = 1e-6)
#> [1] TRUE

Modeling the scale

A parameter is named on the left of its own equation, after a bar:

f2 <- statmod(y ~ x | sigma ~ x, distrib = gaussian1_distrib(), data = da)
lapply(coef(f2), round, digits = 3)
#> $mu
#> (Intercept)           x 
#>       1.008       0.795 
#> 
#> $sigma
#> (Intercept)           x 
#>      -0.575       0.356

The truth is μ=1+0.8x\mu = 1 + 0.8x and log⁡σ=−0.6+0.35x\log\sigma = -0.6 + 0.35x. The equation of the scale is on the log scale, which is the link of that parameter: an equation is fitted on the scale that keeps its parameter inside its domain, so a combination of covariates cannot produce a negative standard deviation.

The log-likelihoods of the two fits show the gain from the second equation:

c(constant_scale = loglik(f1), modeled_scale = loglik(f2))
#> constant_scale  modeled_scale 
#>      -349.8797      -245.7139

Terms

Any modelterms7 term goes in any equation. A smooth carries a penalty, and its smoothing parameter is estimated from the data:

db <- data.frame(z = sort(runif(n, min = -3, max = 3)),
                 g = factor(rep(1:20, length.out = n)))
db$y <- rnorm(n, mean = 1 + sin(1.4 * db$z) + rnorm(20, sd = 0.6)[db$g], sd = 0.4)

f3 <- statmod(y ~ s(z, bspline_smooth(k = 8)),
              distrib = gaussian1_distrib(), data = db)
f3@edf
#>   parameter                        term coefficients      edf
#> 1        mu                      linpar            1 1.000000
#> 2        mu s(z, bspline_smooth(k = 8))            7 5.263947
#> 3     sigma                      linpar            1 1.000000

The smooth has 7 coefficients and uses about 5.3 of them. This effective number of degrees of freedom is the one that a criterion counts, in place of the number of coefficients. hyper() reports the hyperparameters and the source of each:

hyper(f3)
#>   parameter                        term   name estimate  held source   id
#> 1        mu s(z, bspline_smooth(k = 8)) lambda 1.064316 FALSE   reml <NA>

A random effect is written the same way and is fitted by the same machinery, and its penalty is a Gaussian prior over the group effects:

f4 <- statmod(y ~ s(z, bspline_smooth(k = 8)) + random(~ 1 | g),
              distrib = gaussian1_distrib(), data = db)
f4@edf
#>   parameter                        term coefficients       edf
#> 1        mu                      linpar            1  1.000000
#> 2        mu s(z, bspline_smooth(k = 8))            7  6.081977
#> 3        mu              random(~1 | g)           20 18.540158
#> 4     sigma                      linpar            1  1.000000
hyper(f4)
#>   parameter                        term   name  estimate  held source   id
#> 1        mu s(z, bspline_smooth(k = 8)) lambda 1.0345354 FALSE   reml <NA>
#> 2        mu              random(~1 | g)  sigma 0.7070243 FALSE   reml <NA>

The 20 group effects spend about 18.5 degrees of freedom here, and the estimated prior scale is 0.71, against the 0.6 used to draw the groups. A random intercept is a ridge penalty on an indicator block, so it is fitted like a smooth.

Who chooses the hyperparameters

Every hyperparameter is estimated unless the term holds it. The criterion is set by the arguments outer_criterion and sparse_criterion of statmod(). The argument outer_criterion applies to the hyperparameters of a penalty that is twice differentiable, such as a smooth or a random effect:

  • reml() and ml() are marginal criteria. They integrate out the penalized coefficients and are differentiable, so the search uses an exact gradient and, where it exists, an exact Hessian. reml() is the default.
  • aic() and bic() score an estimate of prediction error instead.

A penalty with a kink (lasso(), enet(), scad() and mcp()) is chosen along a path of its own values, from the value that empties the block downwards, and the path is scored by sparse_criterion. This argument is bic() by default and may be aic() or cv(), and a marginal criterion is rejected there. A marginal criterion expands the penalized objective around the penalized mode, and for a lasso that mode lies at the kink, where the second derivative does not exist. The function cv() serves only as sparse_criterion.

A term holds a hyperparameter when the call names its value, for example lasso(x, lambda = 3) or s(z, bspline_smooth(k = 8), hyper = c(lambda = 2)), and the held column of hyper() then reports TRUE:

f5 <- statmod(y ~ s(z, bspline_smooth(k = 8), hyper = c(lambda = 2)),
              distrib = gaussian1_distrib(), data = db)
hyper(f5)
#>   parameter                                               term   name estimate
#> 1        mu s(z, bspline_smooth(k = 8), hyper = c(lambda = 2)) lambda        2
#>   held source   id
#> 1 TRUE  fixed <NA>

Reading a fit 

summary(f3)
#> A statmod fit
#> 
#> Call:  statmod(formula = y ~ s(z, bspline_smooth(k = 8)), distrib = gaussian1_distrib(), 
#>             data = db)
#> 
#> Distribution: gaussian1     Observations: 300
#> 
#> === mu   [identity link]
#> 
#> Parametric terms
#>                estimate      se     z       p  lower upper
#>   (Intercept)    0.9152 0.04728 19.36 < 1e-16 0.8225 1.008
#> 
#> s(z, bspline_smooth(k = 8))   [7 coefficients, edf 5.26]
#>                  estimate      se     z        p   lower  upper
#>   lambda [reml]     1.064  0.7107                 0.2875   3.94
#>   lin              0.1389 0.04736 2.933 0.003361 0.04606 0.2317
#> 
#> === sigma   [log link]
#> 
#> Parametric terms
#>                estimate      se      z         p   lower   upper
#>   (Intercept)   -0.1998 0.04124 -4.844 1.273e-06 -0.2806 -0.1189
#> 
#> 95% intervals, bayesian variance
#> conditional log-likelihood -362.616546    effective df 7.26
#> cAIC 739.761    cBIC 766.665
#> fitted in 206 ms
#> inner   max |grad|/se 3.7e-16   min eigen 1
#> outer   max |grad|/se 2.1e-08   min eigen 0.99
#> 1 note: print(summary(fit), notes = TRUE)

The log-likelihood is the conditional one, read at the fitted coefficients, and the effective degrees of freedom go with it: cAIC and cBIC are built from that pair, and comparing a conditional log-likelihood with a marginal one from another package compares two different quantities. The interval of a hyperparameter, such as a smoothing parameter or a prior standard deviation, is built on the scale that keeps it positive and mapped back, so it cannot contain a negative number, while the interval of a coefficient is on the link scale of its equation. The last lines, headed inner and outer, give the largest gradient in standard errors and the smallest eigenvalue of the curvature for the coefficients and for the hyperparameters, and both are read at the point that the fit reached.

The certificate

The convergence flag of an optimizer records whether a stopping rule fired. statmod_certificate() tests a different property: whether the point reported is a mode of the penalized objective and a stationary point of the criterion in the hyperparameters.

cert <- statmod_certificate(f4)
c(state = cert$state, mode_error = signif(cert$mode_error, digits = 3))
#>       state  mode_error 
#> "converged"  "4.93e-30"

mode_error is how far above its own penalized mode the inner fit stopped, in log-likelihood units, so one limit serves every model whatever its scale. The state is converged; boundary, where a hyperparameter or an estimated coefficient lies at an edge of its range with the criterion flat in it, or the outer curvature has a flat direction; not converged; or unknown, where the derivatives that the certificate needs cannot be computed.

Prediction, and the ordinary generics

predict() returns one compartment per parameter, with a standard error on request:

nd <- data.frame(z = c(-1, 0, 1),
                 g = factor(c(1, 2, 3), levels = levels(db$g)))
predict(f4, newdata = nd, se = TRUE)$mu
#>          fit        se      lower       upper
#> 1 -0.2837629 0.1188442 -0.5166933 -0.05083242
#> 2  1.8468308 0.1199288  1.6117747  2.08188691
#> 3  2.4646126 0.1219674  2.2255610  2.70366431

Prediction reapplies each term’s build_info instead of rebuilding it, so the knots of a smooth and the levels of a factor are those of the fitted model. As a consequence, predicting at rows that were used to fit the model returns the fitted values there.

The generics of stats apply to a fit:

c(nobs = nobs(f4), df.residual = df.residual(f4))
#>        nobs df.residual 
#>    300.0000    273.3779
length(sigma(f4))
#> [1] 300

sigma() returns the standard deviation of the response at each observation, so it is a vector wherever the scale is modeled or the variance depends on the mean. df.residual() subtracts the effective count of degrees of freedom from the number of observations, so it is not an integer.

Three generics signal an error, and each error message names the function to use instead. terms() fails because a fit has one set of terms per distribution parameter, model.frame() fails because a fit keeps the build_info of each term and not the data, and anova() fails because a penalized fit whose hyperparameters were chosen from the same data has no null distribution against which to test.

Simulating from a model

rstatmod() draws from a model at coefficients supplied by the caller, as a simulation study needs:

sim <- rstatmod(y ~ x, distrib = gaussian1_distrib(), data = da,
                par = list(mu = c(1, 0.8), sigma = -0.6))
names(sim)
#> [1] "data"       "par"        "theta"      "latent"     "structural"
#> [6] "hyper"      "n_sim"      "call"
head(sim$data, n = 3)
#>           x          y
#> 1 -2.921535 -1.6210728
#> 2 -2.919658 -0.3713365
#> 3 -2.860013 -1.1992527

It returns the true parameters beside the data and not as an attribute of the data. An attribute survives a row subset without being subset itself, so if the parameters were stored in attr(sim$data, "theta"), the result of attr(sim$data[1:10, ], "theta") would still hold every row’s parameters and would be misaligned with the rows kept.

Summary

  • One formula, in which the equations are separated by a bar, one per distribution parameter; an equation that is omitted is an intercept.
  • Each equation is fitted on the link scale of its parameter, so a combination of covariates cannot leave the domain of the parameter.
  • coef(), predict() and summary() return one compartment per parameter.
  • Any modelterms7 term goes in any equation, and its penalty travels with it.
  • Hyperparameters are estimated unless a term holds one: by reml() or ml() (or aic() or bic()) as outer_criterion where the penalty is twice differentiable, and along a path scored by sparse_criterion (bic() by default, or aic() or cv()) where it has a kink.
  • The log-likelihood reported is the conditional one, and cAIC and cBIC use the effective degrees of freedom and not a parameter count.
  • statmod_certificate() tests whether the point is a mode of the model, which the flag of the optimizer does not do.
